verses.text: These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah:
It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out.
As the heavens are high and the earth is deep, so the hearts of kings cannot be searched.
Remove the dross from the silver, and a vessel for a silversmith will come forth.
Remove the wicked from the king's presence, and his throne will be established in righteousness.
Do not exalt yourself in the presence of the king, and do not stand in the place of great men;
for it is better that he says to you, "Come up here!" than that you should be demoted in the presence of the prince. Even what you have seen with your own eyes,
do not bring hastily to court. Otherwise, what will you do in the end when your neighbor puts you to shame?
Argue your case with your neighbor without betraying another's confidence,
lest the one who hears may disgrace you, and your infamy never go away.
A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver.
Like an earring of gold or an ornament of fine gold is a wise man's rebuke to a listening ear.
Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a trustworthy messenger to those who send him; he refreshes the soul of his masters.
Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given.
Through patience a ruler can be persuaded, and a gentle tongue can break a bone.
If you find honey, eat just what you need, lest you have too much and vomit it up.
Seldom set foot in your neighbor's house, lest he grow weary and hate you.
Like a club or sword or sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor.
Like a broken tooth or a foot out of joint is confidence in a faithless man in time of trouble.
Like one who removes a garment on a cold day or vinegar poured on a wound is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.
If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink.
For in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head, and the LORD will reward you.
As the north wind brings forth rain, so a backbiting tongue brings angry looks.
Better to live on a corner of the roof than to share a house with a quarrelsome wife.
Like cold water to a weary soul is good news from a distant land.
Like a muddied spring or a polluted well is a righteous man who gives way to the wicked.
It is not good to eat too much honey or to search out one's own glory.
Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his temper.

context.author: Solomon; these proverbs “were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah” (25:1), about 250 years after Solomon
context.genre: Wisdom sayings: comparisons, word pictures and contrasts
context.audience: The people of Judah, and especially those who served the king (25:2-7)
context.setting: A new heading: “These are additional proverbs of Solomon, which were copied by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah” (v.1). The collection opens with the king: “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out” (v.2). Do not push yourself forward in the king’s presence; it is better to be told, “Come up here!” (vv.6-7). Many of these sayings are word pictures: “A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver” (v.11); a boaster is like clouds and wind without rain (v.14); good news from far away is like cold water to a weary soul (v.25). Then a great command: if your enemy is hungry, feed him, “for in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head” (vv.21-22).
context.custom: Hezekiah reigned in Jerusalem about 715-686 BC, more than two centuries after Solomon. His court had royal scribes (2 Kings 18:18), and his reign saw a revival of worship and learning (2 Chronicles 29-31). Snow from the mountains cooled drinks at harvest time (v.13), a rare luxury. Burning coals carried in a pan on the head may have been a sign of repentance in Egypt, or the coals may picture the shame that kindness brings.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 26 holds the book’s sharpest sayings about the fool, the slacker and the gossip.
context.timelineBible: Hezekiah “did what was right in the eyes of the LORD” (2 Kings 18:3) and organized the Temple worship and the Levites’ singing (2 Chronicles 29:25-30). Jesus’ parable of the wedding guests (Luke 14:8-10) retells vv.6-7, and Paul quotes vv.21-22 in Romans 12:20. Jude 12 calls false teachers “clouds without water” (Jude 1:12), as in v.14.

translation.meaning: To move, to transfer. Hezekiah’s men moved Solomon’s sayings from an older source into this collection.
To hide. God’s glory is in what he hides; the king’s is in searching it out.
A rare word, perhaps “at the right time” or “in the right way,” like a wheel turning.

gospelParallels.note: Take the last place, and your host will say, “Friend, move up to a better place.”
Paul quotes vv.21-22: if your enemy is hungry, feed him.
Clouds without water, carried along by the wind.

otBackground.note: Hezekiah trusts the LORD and prospers.
Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder serve Hezekiah.

overview.summary: Hezekiah’s scribes add more of Solomon’s proverbs: about kings, humility, fitting words, self-control and kindness to an enemy.
overview.settingLine: Scribes copy Solomon’s sayings for Hezekiah.

history.t: Shebna and others served the court.

archaeology.t: Hebrew writing from Hezekiah’s tunnel, about 700 BC.
A clay seal impression naming Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah, was found in the Ophel excavations just south of the Temple Mount and announced in 2015.

overview.discussion: “If your enemy is hungry, give him food to eat” (v.21). Who is the person I find it hardest to be kind to, and what would one act of kindness look like?
overview.book: The book of Proverbs · 31 chapters. Short sayings and longer poems that teach how to live wisely in God’s world, beginning with the fear of the LORD.
overview.author: Solomon (25:1)
